content: Scalp rashes are relatively straightforward to diagnose, particularly when caused by conditions such as scalp dermatitis or infections. However, their treatment can be more challenging. In many cases, topical therapy alone may not suffice, and a combination of topical and systemic therapies over extended periods may be necessary to achieve and maintain complete control of the condition. When differentiating a scalp rash from other diseases, it is important to consider the following conditions in alphabetical order: Contact dermatitis Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp Discoid lupus Kerion Psoriasis Scalp folliculitis Seborrheic dermatitis Tinea capitis Diagnosis History and Symptoms Seborrheic dermatitis: This condition typically presents as diffuse, white, and non-adherent scaling on the scalp. Bacterial folliculitis: Diagnosis can be confirmed by examining an intact pustule on the scalp. Laboratory Findings A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation can be performed in the clinical setting to identify fungal spores within the hair shaft. Fungal cultures can be obtained from the site of a kerion or scalp scaling to rule out tinea capitis. It is critical to ensure that the hair root is intact when collecting samples. A shave biopsy should not be performed indiscriminately. However, when appropriately utilized, it can assist in diagnosing seborrheic dermatitis.
